walkthroughs.body_html:
Enzymes are biological catalysts.

They speed up chemical reactions in your body so they happen at a useful rate — at body temperature, not in a furnace.

They are proteins, made of folded chains of amino acids.

Each enzyme has a special pocket called the active site.

The substrate fits into the active site like a key fits a lock — only the right shape will do.

The enzyme then breaks the substrate apart (or joins pieces together) into the product, and the enzyme is freed to do it again.

This is the lock-and-key model.

Most enzymes end in -ase and are named after their substrate.

- Sucrose → sucrase
- Maltose → maltase
- Lactose → lactase
- Lipids → lipase
- Proteins → protease

Spot the pattern: take the substrate name, swap the ending for -ase.
